questions.prompt: In strict mode, what is `this` inside a function called as a bare call?

query.title: Bare calls have undefined this in strict mode
query.explanation: In strict mode, a function called as a bare call has `this` set to `undefined`. The call has no receiver, and strict mode does not substitute the global object. That substitution is the sloppy-mode behavior, so the global object, `null`, and the function itself are the wrong readings.

questions.prompt: What does `obj.m()` return?
questions.code:
const obj = { n: 1, m() { return this.n; } };
obj.m();

query.title: A method call binds this to the receiver
query.explanation: A method call `obj.m()` sets `this` to the receiver in front of the dot, so `this.n` is `1`. The function is not bare, so strict mode does not make `this` undefined. The call expression supplies the receiver; the function object itself is not `this`.

questions.prompt: In strict mode, what is `this` when an extracted method is called as a bare function?

query.title: Extracting a method drops the receiver
query.syntax:
const fn = obj.m;
fn(); // undefined in strict mode
query.explanation: `this` is set by the call, not stored on the function when it is created as a method. Copying `obj.m` into `fn` and calling `fn()` is a bare call, so strict mode sets `this` to `undefined`. The object is not remembered, and the global object is not filled in.

questions.prompt: What does `f.call({ n: 2 })` return?
questions.code:
function f() { return this.n; }
f.call({ n: 2 });

query.title: call sets this for that call
query.explanation: `Function.prototype.call` invokes the function with its first argument as `this` and any further arguments as parameters. Here `this.n` is `2` for that call only. A bare call would not see that object, and `call` does not permanently rebind `f`.

questions.prompt: What does `f.apply({ n: 1 }, [2, 3])` return?
questions.code:
function f(a, b) { return this.n + a + b; }
f.apply({ n: 1 }, [2, 3]);

query.title: apply sets this and takes an argument array
query.explanation: `apply` sets `this` from its first argument and expands the second argument as the parameter list. `this.n + a + b` is `1 + 2 + 3`, which is `6`. It does not pass the array as a single parameter, and it does not ignore `this`.

questions.prompt: What does the bound function `g()` return?

query.title: bind returns a new function with this locked
query.explanation: `bind` returns a new function whose `this` is fixed to the object you pass. Calling `g` with no receiver still reads `n` as `5`. `bind` does not mutate `f`, and the new function does not fall back to `undefined` or the global object.

questions.prompt: What does `g.call({ n: 99 })` return after `g` was created with `bind`?

query.title: call cannot override a bound this
query.syntax:
const g = f.bind({ n: 1 });
g.call({ n: 99 }); // 1
query.explanation: A function produced by `bind` ignores a later `this` from `call` or `apply`. The bound object stays the receiver, so the result is `1`, not `99`. `call` still forwards extra arguments, but it cannot replace `[[BoundThis]]`.

questions.prompt: What does `outer.call({ tag: "outer" })` return?

query.title: An arrow ignores this passed to call
query.syntax:
const arrow = () => this;
arrow.call(other); // still the outer this
query.explanation: An arrow function takes `this` from the enclosing scope, here `outer`, and `arrow.call` cannot replace it. `outer` was invoked with `{ tag: "outer" }`, so the arrow reads that tag. The object passed to `arrow.call` is not the arrow `this`.

questions.prompt: What does `obj.m()` return?

query.title: An arrow inside a method sees that method this
query.explanation: The method call sets `this` to `obj`, and the arrow captures that lexical `this`. `inner` therefore reads `obj.n`, which is `1`. The arrow does not get its own receiver, and it does not reset `this` to `undefined`.

questions.prompt: What does `obj.get()` return?

query.title: An arrow property does not receive the object
query.syntax:
const obj = { get: () => this };
obj.get(); // not obj
query.explanation: An arrow stored on an object still uses the `this` of the scope where it was created. `make` was called with `{ tag: "outer" }`, so `obj.get()` returns `"outer"`, not `"obj"`. Property lookup does not bind `this` for an arrow the way a method call binds `this` for a normal function.

questions.prompt: What is `new Box(4).n`?
questions.code:
function Box(n) { this.n = n; }
new Box(4).n;

query.title: new binds this to the new instance
query.syntax:
function Box(n) { this.n = n; }
new Box(4);
query.explanation: `new` creates an object and calls the constructor with `this` set to that object, including in strict mode. The assignment `this.n = n` therefore lands on the instance, and the read is `4`. A constructor call is not a bare call, so `this` is not `undefined` and the property is not written to the global object.

questions.prompt: What does `f()` return?

query.title: A closure sees later assignments
query.explanation: A closure keeps the binding, not a copy of the value from the moment the function was created. `f` reads `n` when it runs, after the assignment `n = 2`, so the result is `2`. It does not snapshot `1`, and `n` is still in scope.

questions.prompt: What does `fns.map((fn) => fn())` produce?

query.title: var in a for loop is one binding
query.syntax: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i);
query.explanation: `var` declares one function-scoped binding for the whole loop, and the loop leaves `i` at `3`. Every closure reads that same binding, so each call returns `3`. The closures do not capture `0`, `1`, and `2` as separate values.

questions.prompt: What does `fns.map((fn) => fn())` produce?

query.title: let in a for loop creates a binding per iteration
query.syntax: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) fns.push(() => i);
query.explanation: A `for` loop with `let` creates a fresh binding of `i` for each iteration. Each closure closes over the binding from its own iteration, so the calls return `0`, `1`, and `2`. This is not the single shared `var` binding that every closure would read as `3`.

questions.prompt: What does `outer(7)()` return?

query.title: A returned function keeps the outer parameter
query.explanation: The inner function closes over the parameter `x`, and returning it does not drop that environment. `outer(7)` finishes, but the returned function still reads `7`. Parameters are not wiped when the outer call returns, and `x` is not `undefined` on the later call.

questions.prompt: What is `obj.a`?

query.title: A missing own property is found on the prototype
query.syntax:
const obj = Object.create(proto);
obj.a; // found on proto
query.explanation: Property lookup walks the prototype chain when the object has no own property of that name. `obj` does not own `a`, so the read finds `proto.a`, which is `1`. A missing own property is not automatically `undefined` while a prototype still has it.

questions.prompt: After `obj.a = 2`, what is `obj.a`?

query.title: An own property shadows an inherited one
query.explanation: Assigning `obj.a = 2` creates an own data property, and lookup stops there. The read is `2` even though `proto.a` is still `1`. The assignment does not rewrite the prototype property, and the inherited value does not keep winning.

questions.prompt: What is `a.m === b.m` for two instances of this class?

choices.text: false, because each instance owns a fresh method
true, because both share the method on the prototype
false, because methods live on the constructor
true, because the method is copied onto each instance at the first call

query.title: A class method lives on the prototype
query.syntax:
class Box { m() {} }
a.m === b.m; // true
query.explanation: A class method is defined once on `Box.prototype`, and instances share that function. `a.m` and `b.m` are the same reference, so the comparison is `true`. Class methods are not installed as own properties per instance, and they are not stored on the constructor.

questions.prompt: Where does the class field `n` live?

choices.text: on Box.prototype, shared by every instance
as an own property of each instance
only inside the class body, not on the instance

query.title: A class field is an own property of each instance
query.syntax:
class Box { n = 1; }
Object.hasOwn(new Box(), "n"); // true
query.explanation: A public class field is installed on the new instance during construction, so `Object.hasOwn(a, "n")` is true and `Box.prototype` does not own `n`. Changing `a.n` leaves `b.n` at `1`. The field is not a shared prototype property the way a method is.

questions.prompt: Where does `static id` live?

choices.text: on the constructor, not on the prototype
as an own property of each instance
only while the class body is evaluating

query.title: A static method lives on the constructor
query.explanation: A static method is a property of the constructor function, so `Box.id` is the function and `Box.prototype.id` is `undefined`. Instances do not receive it as an own field, and it is not found by walking the instance prototype chain. Subclasses can still inherit static methods through the constructor chain.

questions.prompt: What happens when `new Child()` runs?

choices.text: The instance is created and n is 1

query.title: A derived constructor must call super before using this
query.explanation: In a derived constructor, `this` is uninitialized until `super()` returns. Reading or writing `this` before that call throws a `ReferenceError`, even if `super()` appears later in the same constructor. The later `super()` call does not retroactively make the earlier access legal.

questions.prompt: What does `new Child().m()` return?

query.title: super.method calls the parent method
query.explanation: `super.m()` looks up `m` on the parent prototype and calls that function, so the return value is `"parent"`. The override in `Child` does not make `super.m` recurse into itself. The parent method still runs with the child instance as `this`.

questions.prompt: What is `new Child() instanceof Base`?

choices.text: false, because only Child constructed it
false, because instanceof checks one level only
true, because instanceof walks the prototype chain

query.title: instanceof walks the prototype chain
query.explanation: `instanceof` tests whether `Base.prototype` appears anywhere on the instance prototype chain, not only as the direct prototype. `Child.prototype` inherits from `Base.prototype`, so the result is `true`. It is not limited to the constructor that was actually invoked with `new`.

questions.prompt: What is the value of `obj.toString`?
questions.code:
const obj = Object.create(null);
obj.toString;

choices.text: a TypeError is thrown by the read

query.title: Object.create(null) has no Object.prototype methods
query.explanation: `Object.create(null)` sets the prototype to `null`, so the object does not inherit `toString` or other `Object.prototype` methods. Reading `obj.toString` yields `undefined`. The read itself does not throw; calling that missing property would throw a `TypeError`.

questions.prompt: What does `Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)` return?

query.title: Object.getPrototypeOf returns the prototype
query.explanation: `Object.getPrototypeOf` reads the internal prototype slot, which `Object.create` set to `proto`. The result is that same object, not `Object.prototype`, unless that happens to be the prototype. Plain objects do not have a `.prototype` property; `.prototype` lives on constructor functions.

questions.prompt: When does the callback passed to `.then` or `.catch` run?
questions.code: Promise.resolve(1).then((value) => value);

choices.text: as a microtask, after the current stack

query.title: Promise reactions are microtasks
query.explanation: A `.then` or `.catch` callback is queued as a microtask, so it runs after the current call stack clears and before timer tasks. `then` itself returns immediately and does not run the callback on the current stack. The callback is not a `setTimeout` macrotask.

questions.prompt: What kind of task is a `setTimeout(fn, 0)` callback?
questions.code: setTimeout(() => {}, 0);

choices.text: synchronous code on the current stack

query.title: setTimeout callbacks are macrotasks
query.explanation: `setTimeout` schedules a macrotask, also called a task, even when the delay is `0`. It does not run before the current stack ends, and it does not jump the microtask queue. A delay of `0` is not the same mechanism as `Promise.then` or `queueMicrotask`.

questions.prompt: After the timer callback has run, what is `log`?

query.title: Sync code, then microtasks, then timers
query.explanation: The current script runs to the end first, so `"sync"` is pushed before either callback. The promise reaction is a microtask and runs next. The timer is a macrotask, so it runs only after that microtask, which is why the log is `"sync"`, `"micro"`, `"timer"`.

questions.prompt: What does calling `f()` return?
questions.code:
async function f() { return 1; }
f();

query.title: An async function always returns a promise
query.syntax:
async function f() { return 1; }
f() instanceof Promise; // true
query.explanation: Calling an async function always hands back a promise, even when the body returns a plain value. That promise fulfills with `1`; the call itself is not the number `1`. A throw inside the function rejects that promise instead of changing the call into a non-promise return.

questions.prompt: Immediately after `f()` returns and the next line runs, before microtasks, what is `log`?

query.title: An async function runs synchronously until its first await
query.explanation: The body runs on the caller stack until the first `await`, so `"body"` is logged before `f()` returns. `await` schedules the rest as a microtask, and only then does the caller push `"caller"`. `"after"` is not in the log yet; it does not run before the async call returns.

questions.prompt: What does `await 1` do inside an async function?

choices.text: It blocks the caller until a timer fires
It throws, because 1 is not a promise
It wraps 1 and resumes later as a microtask with that value
It continues on the same stack before the async call returns

query.title: await on a non-promise still resumes as a microtask
query.syntax: const value = await 1; // value is 1, later
query.explanation: `await` on a non-promise wraps it with promise resolution and resumes the async function as a microtask. The awaited value is `1`, and the returned promise fulfills with `1`. The continuation does not keep running on the caller stack, and a non-promise is not a thrown error.

questions.prompt: What happens at the call `f()`?
questions.code:
async function f() { throw new Error("x"); }
f();

choices.text: The returned promise rejects, and the caller is not thrown into
The caller catches a synchronous exception
The call returns a fulfilled promise of the error object

query.title: throw inside an async function rejects its promise
query.syntax:
async function f() { throw new Error("x"); }
// f() rejects; it does not throw into the caller
query.explanation: A `throw` in an async function rejects the promise that the call returned. A `try/catch` around the bare call `f()` does not see a synchronous exception. The call still returns a promise; it does not return `undefined` or a fulfilled promise of the error.

questions.prompt: What happens to this `Promise.all` call?

choices.text: It waits for every input and then fulfills
It rejects with the first rejection reason

query.title: Promise.all rejects on the first rejection
query.explanation: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as one input rejects, using that rejection reason. It does not fulfill with a partial list and it does not wait to turn the rejection into a settled status object. Other inputs may still settle later, but their results are not the result of `Promise.all`.

questions.prompt: What does `Promise.allSettled` do when one input rejects?

choices.text: It fulfills with one result object per input
It fulfills with only the fulfilled values

query.title: Promise.allSettled waits and does not reject for an input
query.explanation: `Promise.allSettled` waits for every input and fulfills with a status object for each one, including `{ status: "rejected", reason }` for a rejection. An input rejection does not reject the `allSettled` promise. It does not drop rejected inputs or return only the fulfillment values.

questions.prompt: What does this `Promise.race` call do?

query.title: Promise.race settles with the first settlement
query.explanation: `Promise.race` adopts whichever input settles first. The already fulfilled promise wins, so the race fulfills with `"fast"` and does not wait for the pending input. If the first settlement had been a rejection, the race would reject with that reason instead.

questions.prompt: What does `Promise.any` do when every input rejects?

query.title: Promise.any fulfills with the first fulfillment
query.syntax:
Promise.any([rejected, fulfilled]); // fulfills
Promise.any([rejected, rejected]); // AggregateError
query.explanation: `Promise.any` fulfills with the first fulfillment and ignores earlier rejections. If every input rejects, it rejects with an `AggregateError` whose errors are those reasons, not with the first reason alone. It does not fulfill with `undefined` when nothing fulfilled.

questions.prompt: After both callbacks have run, what is `log`?

query.title: queueMicrotask runs before setTimeout of 0
query.explanation: `queueMicrotask` queues a microtask, and `setTimeout(fn, 0)` queues a macrotask. The microtask checkpoint runs the microtask before the timer task, so the log is `"micro"` then `"timer"`. A delay of `0` does not put the timer ahead of an already queued microtask.

questions.prompt: What is `q` relative to `p`?
questions.code:
const p = Promise.resolve(1);
const q = p.then((n) => n);

query.title: then returns a new promise
query.syntax:
const q = p.then((n) => n);
q !== p;
query.explanation: `then` always returns a new promise that follows the callback result. `q` is not `p`, even when the callback returns the same fulfillment value. `then` does not return the callback value directly, and it does not return `undefined`.

questions.prompt: What is the fulfillment value of the promise returned by `.then`?
questions.code: Promise.resolve(1).then((n) => n + 1);

query.title: A non-promise return becomes the next fulfillment
query.explanation: When a `then` callback returns a non-promise, that value becomes the fulfillment value of the promise `then` returned. Here the fulfillment value is `2`, not `1` and not `undefined`. The promise is not fulfilled with another promise object, because the callback did not return a promise.

questions.prompt: What does the promise returned by `.then` do?
questions.code: Promise.resolve(1).then(() => Promise.reject("later"));

choices.text: It fulfills with a rejected promise

query.title: Returning a promise from then adopts it
query.explanation: If a `then` callback returns a promise, the promise returned by `then` adopts it. A returned rejection therefore rejects the chain with `"later"` rather than fulfilling with a promise object. The original fulfillment `1` is not kept once the callback returns a different promise.

questions.prompt: What is the fulfillment value of this promise?
questions.code: Promise.resolve(1).finally(() => 2);

query.title: finally keeps the fulfillment value
query.explanation: `finally` runs the callback and then passes the original fulfillment through, so a returned `2` is ignored and the promise fulfills with `1`. The callback return does not replace the value the way a `then` return does. If `finally` throws or returns a rejected promise, that rejection replaces the result.

questions.prompt: What does the first `it.next()` return?

query.title: next runs a generator to the next yield
query.explanation: The first `next` starts the generator and runs it until the first `yield`, then returns the iterator result `{ value: 1, done: false }`. It does not return the bare number `1`, and it does not continue through later yields in the same call. `done` becomes `true` only after the generator finishes.

questions.prompt: What does `it.next(5)` return?

query.title: next(value) supplies the yield expression
query.syntax:
const x = yield 1;
it.next(5); // x is 5
query.explanation: The value passed to the `next` that resumes a `yield` becomes the value of that `yield` expression. After the opening `next` pauses at `yield 1`, `it.next(5)` assigns `5` to `x` and the generator returns it, so the result is `{ value: 5, done: true }`. The argument to the first `next` is discarded because no `yield` is waiting yet.

questions.prompt: Which method does `for...of` call to obtain an iterator?

query.title: for...of uses Symbol.iterator
query.explanation: `for...of` gets an iterator by calling the iterable `Symbol.iterator` method, then calls `next` on the result. `Symbol.asyncIterator` is what `for await...of` uses, not `for...of`. `Object.keys` and `toString` are not consulted to start the loop.

questions.prompt: What happens when this loop runs?
questions.code: for (const item of { a: 1 }) {}

query.title: A plain object is not iterable
query.explanation: A plain object has no `Symbol.iterator`, so it is not iterable. `for...of` throws a `TypeError` instead of walking keys or values. The loop does not succeed with zero iterations; iteration fails when the iterator method is missing.

questions.prompt: What shape does an iterator `next()` method return?

query.title: The iterator protocol is { value, done }
query.explanation: The iterator protocol says `next` returns an object with `value` and `done`. `done: true` means the iterator is finished. `next` does not return the bare value, and the result object is not the iterator itself, which is the object that has a `next` method.

questions.prompt: What is `[...map.keys()]`?

query.title: Map iterates in insertion order
query.explanation: `Map` iteration follows insertion order, including for numeric keys. The keys come back as `2` then `1`, not sorted as `1` then `2`. Map does not reorder integer-like keys the way ordinary object key order does, and the spread of `keys()` is the keys, not the values.

questions.prompt: What does `map.get(key)` return?

query.title: Map can use an object as a key by identity
query.explanation: `Map` accepts object keys and compares them by identity. `get` with the same object reference returns `1`. Object keys are allowed; `Map` does not require primitive keys and does not throw for a plain object.

questions.prompt: What does `map.get({ a: 1 })` return?

query.title: Map does not match a different object with the same contents
query.explanation: Object keys are compared with SameValueZero identity, not by deep equality of their properties. The object passed to `get` is a different reference from the object passed to `set`, so the lookup is `undefined`. Equal contents do not make the keys the same entry.

questions.prompt: What is `set.size` after adding `NaN` twice?

query.title: Set treats NaN as the same value
query.explanation: `Set` uses SameValueZero, and under that comparison `NaN` matches `NaN`. The second `add` does not create another entry, so `size` is `1`. The `NaN !== NaN` comparison does not control `Set` membership.

questions.prompt: What happens when a string is used as a WeakMap key?
questions.code: new WeakMap().set("user", 1);

choices.text: The entry is stored under that string
The string is boxed into a String object and stored
The entry is stored until the next garbage collection

query.title: A primitive WeakMap key throws
query.explanation: WeakMap keys must be objects or unregistered symbols, because those are the values that can be held weakly. A string is neither, so `set` throws a `TypeError`. The string is not boxed into a `String` object for you, and it is not stored the way a `Map` key would be.

questions.prompt: What does spreading a WeakMap do?
questions.code: const entries = [...new WeakMap()];

query.title: WeakMap is not iterable
query.explanation: `WeakMap` has no `Symbol.iterator`, no `keys`, no `forEach`, and no `size`. Spreading it throws a `TypeError` because it is not iterable. It does not produce an empty array; the entries are intentionally not exposed.

questions.prompt: What is `Symbol("a") === Symbol("a")`?
questions.code: Symbol("a") === Symbol("a");

choices.text: true, because symbols with one description are interned
true, but only inside the same function
false, because each Symbol() call creates a new symbol

query.title: Symbol() creates a unique symbol
query.explanation: Each `Symbol()` call creates a new symbol. The description is only a label, so two calls with `"a"` are not equal. `Symbol()` does not intern by description; that is what `Symbol.for` does.

questions.prompt: What is `Symbol.for("a") === Symbol.for("a")`?
questions.code: Symbol.for("a") === Symbol.for("a");

choices.text: true, the registry returns the same symbol
true, but only within one function

query.title: Symbol.for returns a shared registry symbol
query.explanation: `Symbol.for` looks up a key in the global symbol registry and creates the symbol only if that key is missing. A second call with `"a"` returns the same symbol, so the comparison is `true`. It does not behave like `Symbol()`, which never consults the registry.

questions.prompt: What does `Object.keys` return for this object?
questions.code:
const s = Symbol("s");
Object.keys({ [s]: 1, a: 2 });

query.title: Object.keys omits symbol keys
query.explanation: `Object.keys` returns an array of the object own enumerable string keys. Symbol keys are omitted, so the result is `["a"]`. It does not throw because of the symbol, and it does not include the symbol in the array.

questions.prompt: What does `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` return?
questions.code:
const s = Symbol("s");
Object.getOwnPropertySymbols({ [s]: 1, a: 2 });

query.title: Object.getOwnPropertySymbols returns symbol keys
query.explanation: `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols` returns the object own symbol keys, here `[s]`. String keys are left out, including enumerable ones such as `"a"`. `Object.keys` is the opposite filter: strings only, no symbols.

questions.prompt: What does `Number(obj)` return?

query.title: Symbol.toPrimitive handles coercion hints
query.explanation: When `Symbol.toPrimitive` is present, coercion calls it with a hint and uses the primitive it returns. `Number(obj)` passes the hint `"number"`, so the result is `7`. `valueOf` and `toString` are not consulted once `Symbol.toPrimitive` handles the conversion.

questions.prompt: What is `[10, 2, 1].sort()`?

query.title: The default sort comparator compares strings
query.explanation: The default comparator converts each element to a string and compares those strings. `"1"` is before `"10"`, and `"10"` is before `"2"`, so the order is `1`, `10`, `2`. It does not compare the numbers numerically unless you pass a numeric comparator.

questions.prompt: After `const b = a.sort()`, what is true?
questions.code:
const a = [3, 1];
const b = a.sort();

choices.text: a is still [3, 1] and b is [1, 3]
a and b are the same array, now [1, 3]
b is [1, 3] and a is unchanged

query.title: sort mutates the array in place
query.syntax:
const b = a.sort();
a === b; // true
query.explanation: `sort` reorders the receiver and returns that same array. After the call, `a` is `[1, 3]` and `a === b`. It does not return a fresh copy; that is what `toSorted` does.

questions.prompt: What is `[10, 2, 1].sort((a, b) => a - b)`?

query.title: A numeric comparator is (a, b) => a - b
query.explanation: A comparator should return a negative number when `a` belongs before `b`. `a - b` does that for ordinary numbers, so the array becomes `[1, 2, 10]`. The default string comparator is not used once this function is passed, so `10` is not placed between `1` and `2`.

questions.prompt: What is `log` after `forEach`?
questions.code:
const log = [];
[1, , 3].forEach((n) => log.push(n));

query.title: forEach skips holes in a sparse array
query.explanation: `forEach` visits indexes that exist and skips holes. The callback runs for `1` and `3` only, so `log` is `[1, 3]`. The hole is not passed to the callback as `undefined`.

questions.prompt: What is true of `[1, , 3].map((n) => n * 2)`?
questions.code: const out = [1, , 3].map((n) => n * 2);

choices.text: The callback runs 3 times and index 1 is undefined
The callback runs 2 times and index 1 stays a hole
The callback runs 2 times and the result is shorter
The callback runs 3 times and index 1 is 0

query.title: map keeps holes and skips their callbacks
query.explanation: `map` does not call the callback for a hole, and the result keeps that hole. The callback runs twice, the length stays `3`, and `1 in out` is false. The hole is not filled with `undefined` or `0`, and the result is not compacted.

questions.prompt: What is `1 in [, ,]`?

choices.text: true, because the hole is undefined
false, because a hole is a missing property

query.title: A hole is a missing index
query.explanation: The array `[ , , ]` has length `2`, but indexes `0` and `1` were never created. `in` looks for a property, so `1 in [, ,]` is false. Length does not mean every index exists, and a hole is not an own property whose value is `undefined`.

questions.prompt: What does `[...[, ,]]` produce?
questions.code: const copy = [...[, ,]];

choices.text: a sparse array that still has holes

query.title: Spreading a hole yields undefined
query.explanation: Array spread uses the iterator, and the array iterator yields `undefined` for a hole. The new array literal stores those values as real elements, so both indexes exist. The holes are not preserved as holes, and the spread is not empty.

questions.prompt: On the first callback of this `reduce`, what is the accumulator?
questions.code: [2, 3, 4].reduce((acc, n) => acc + n);

query.title: reduce without an initial value starts at the first element
query.syntax: [2, 3, 4].reduce((acc, n) => acc + n); // first acc is 2
query.explanation: When `reduce` is given no initial value, it uses the first element as the accumulator and starts the callback at the second element. The first call receives `2` and `3`, not `0` and `2`. An initial value is what would make the first element a callback argument instead of the starting accumulator.

questions.prompt: What does `[].reduce((a, b) => a + b)` do?
questions.code: [].reduce((a, b) => a + b);

query.title: reduce on an empty array with no initial value throws
query.explanation: With no initial value and no first element to use as the accumulator, `reduce` throws a `TypeError`. It does not return `undefined`, `0`, or `null`. Passing an initial value, as in `[].reduce(fn, 0)`, is what returns that initial value for an empty array.

query.title: flat flattens one level by default
query.explanation: `flat()` uses a depth of `1`, so only the outer array is unwrapped. The result is `[1, 2, [3]]`, and the inner `[3]` stays an array. A depth of `2` or `Infinity` would flatten further; the default call does not.

questions.prompt: What is `[1, 2].flatMap((n) => [n, n])`?

query.title: flatMap maps, then flattens one level
query.explanation: `flatMap` maps each element, then flattens the result by one level. Each callback result `[n, n]` is concatenated, producing `[1, 1, 2, 2]`. It is not the same as `map`, which would leave an array of pairs, and it does not flatten more than one level.

questions.prompt: After `const b = a.toSorted()`, what is true?
questions.code:
const a = [3, 1];
const b = a.toSorted();

query.title: toSorted returns a copy
query.explanation: `toSorted` returns a new sorted array and does not mutate the receiver. `a` remains `[3, 1]` and `b` is `[1, 3]`. `sort` is the method that rewrites the original array in place.

query.title: at(-1) returns the last element
query.explanation: `at` counts a negative index from the end, so `-1` is the last element, `"c"`. Bracket access `arr[-1]` does not do that; it looks up the property name `"-1"` and would be `undefined` here. `at` does not throw for a negative index that still lands inside the array.

questions.prompt: A tagged template receives the string parts as its first argument and the interpolations as the remaining arguments.

query.title: Tagged templates pass parts, then values
query.explanation: A tag function is called with the cooked string parts as the first argument, an array that also has a `raw` property. Each interpolation is passed as a following argument. The tag is not called with one string that already has the values spliced in.

questions.prompt: Rest parameters are a real array.

query.title: Rest parameters collect a real array
query.explanation: A rest parameter is created as an `Array` instance, so array methods work on it and `Array.isArray` is true. It contains only the arguments that were not bound to earlier parameters. It is not the array-like `arguments` object.

questions.prompt: The arguments object is array-like, not an Array instance.

query.title: arguments is array-like
query.explanation: `arguments` has indexed elements and a `length`, so it is array-like, but `Array.isArray(arguments)` is false and array methods are not on it. A rest parameter is the way to receive a real array. Treating `arguments` as an `Array` instance is the wrong reading.

questions.prompt: function.length counts parameters before the first parameter that has a default or is a rest parameter.
questions.code:
function f(a, b = 1, c) {}
f.length;

query.title: function.length stops at the first default or rest
query.explanation: `length` is the number of parameters before the first default or rest element. In `f(a, b = 1, c)`, that count is `1`, because `c` sits after a default and is not counted. It is not the total number of named parameters, and a rest parameter is not included.

questions.prompt: new.target is undefined when the function is called without new.

query.title: new.target is undefined without new
query.syntax:
function f() { return new.target; }
f(); // undefined
query.explanation: Inside a function called without `new`, `new.target` is `undefined`. The same function invoked with `new` sees `new.target` set to the constructor that `new` applied. A bare call does not report the function as `new.target`.

questions.prompt: Reading a private field from outside the class that declares it throws.

query.title: Private fields are not readable from outside the class
query.explanation: A private identifier is in scope only inside the class that declares it. Mentioning `#n` outside that class is a `SyntaxError`, not a missing-property read that returns `undefined`. Privacy here is a syntax and brand rule, not an ordinary prototype lookup.

questions.prompt: `#field in object` is the brand check for a private field.

query.title: Private in is the brand check
query.syntax: #n in obj; // true only for instances of this class
query.explanation: `#n in obj` returns true when `obj` carries the private brand for `#n`, and false when it does not. It is the check for that private field, and a missing brand does not throw. Reading `#n` on an unbranded object would throw a `TypeError`; the `in` form is the boolean test.

questions.prompt: Reading a property runs its getter.

query.title: A property read runs the getter
query.explanation: If a property is defined with a getter, a normal read calls that function and uses its return value. The read is not a plain data load that skips the getter. Assignment uses the setter, when there is one, rather than the getter.

questions.prompt: Assigning a property runs its setter.

query.title: A property write runs the setter
query.explanation: If a property has a setter, assignment calls that function with the right-hand side. The value is not stored as an own data property that bypasses the setter. A later read uses the getter, or `undefined` if no getter was defined.

questions.prompt: A non-enumerable property is omitted from Object.keys.

query.title: Object.keys skips non-enumerable properties
query.explanation: `Object.keys` lists own enumerable string keys only. A property defined with `enumerable: false` is left out, so the result is an empty array even though the property exists. `Object.getOwnPropertyNames` would still include that string key.

questions.prompt: Object.freeze is shallow: a nested object can still be mutated.
questions.code:
const obj = Object.freeze({ inner: { n: 1 } });
obj.inner.n = 2;

query.title: Object.freeze does not freeze nested objects
query.syntax:
const obj = Object.freeze({ inner: { n: 1 } });
obj.inner.n = 2; // allowed
query.explanation: `Object.freeze` makes the object own properties non-writable and non-configurable, and it rejects new properties. The object stored in `inner` is a different object and was not frozen, so `obj.inner.n = 2` still works. Freeze is not a deep walk.

questions.prompt: Object.seal allows changing existing properties and forbids adding new ones.

query.title: Object.seal locks the property set
query.explanation: `Object.seal` marks existing properties non-configurable and prevents adding or removing properties. An existing writable property can still be assigned, so `obj.n = 2` works. Adding `obj.m` fails, and in strict mode that assignment throws a `TypeError`.

questions.prompt: structuredClone of a Date produces a Date.
questions.code:
const copy = structuredClone(new Date("2020-01-01T00:00:00Z"));
copy instanceof Date;

query.title: structuredClone preserves Date objects
query.explanation: `structuredClone` copies a `Date` as a `Date` with the same time value, so `instanceof Date` is true. The clone is a different object from the original. This is not the JSON conversion, which turns a `Date` into a string.

questions.prompt: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(a Date)) produces a string, not a Date.
questions.code:
const value = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(new Date("2020-01-01T00:00:00Z")));
typeof value;

query.title: JSON turns a Date into a string
query.explanation: `Date.prototype.toJSON` returns an ISO string, so `JSON.stringify` emits a string and `JSON.parse` parses that string. The result is not a `Date`. `structuredClone` is the copy that keeps the `Date` type.

questions.prompt: structuredClone throws if the value contains a function.
questions.code: structuredClone({ run() {} });

query.title: structuredClone rejects functions
query.explanation: Functions are not part of the structured clone algorithm, so a value that contains one throws a `DataCloneError`. The function is not dropped so the rest can be cloned. The clone fails instead of returning an object that omits `run`.

questions.prompt: A regexp with the g flag remembers lastIndex across exec calls.

query.title: A global regexp keeps lastIndex
query.explanation: `exec` on a global regexp starts at `lastIndex` and writes the index after the match back into `lastIndex`. The next `exec` on that same regexp continues from there instead of from `0`. A regexp without `g` or `y` does not advance a search cursor this way.

questions.prompt: String.prototype.match with a global regexp returns all matches and resets lastIndex to 0.

query.title: match on a global regexp collects every match
query.explanation: `String.prototype.match` on a global regexp sets `lastIndex` to `0`, collects every match, and leaves `lastIndex` at `0` when it finishes. It does not resume from a previous `lastIndex` the way a later `exec` would. The return value is an array of match strings, not one `exec` result.

questions.prompt: A function passed to replace receives the match and its return value is the replacement.
questions.code: "ab".replace("a", (match) => match.toUpperCase());

query.title: replace can take a replacer function
query.explanation: When the replacement is a function, `replace` calls it with the matched text first and uses the function return value as the replacement text. The return value is inserted as text; it is not searched again as a pattern. The function is not ignored in favor of a string pattern.

questions.prompt: An imported live binding sees a later assignment to an exported let.

query.title: Imported let bindings are live
query.explanation: An `import` of an exported `let` is a live binding to that module variable, not a copy taken when the importer loaded. A later assignment in the exporting module is visible to the importer. The import does not freeze the value that was current at evaluation time.

questions.prompt: Import declarations are hoisted, and the imported module is evaluated before the importer module body runs.

query.title: Imports are linked before the module body runs
query.syntax:
import { n } from "./mod.js";
// mod.js has already been evaluated
query.explanation: Import declarations are hoisted to the top of the module, and dependency evaluation finishes before the importer body starts. Code in the importer does not run ahead of the imported module body. The import is not an ordinary statement that waits until the interpreter reaches that line.

questions.prompt: A return inside finally overrides a return inside try.

query.title: A finally return replaces the try return
query.explanation: A `return` in `finally` completes the function with that value, so `f()` returns `2`. The `return 1` in `try` is discarded when `finally` returns. `finally` does not merely run and then let the `try` result win.

questions.prompt: Two let declarations of the same name in one switch, in cases that do not have their own blocks, throw when that code is evaluated because the cases share one scope.

query.title: A switch body is one lexical scope
query.explanation: The `switch` block is a single lexical scope, so both `let x` declarations are in that same scope. Evaluating the code throws a `SyntaxError` for the duplicate lexical binding. Separate blocks around each case would give each `let` its own scope.

questions.prompt: In strict mode, delete of an unqualified identifier is a SyntaxError.

query.title: Strict delete of a bare identifier is a SyntaxError
query.explanation: In strict mode, `delete` applied to an unqualified identifier is an early `SyntaxError`. It does not return `false` and leave the binding in place. `delete obj.prop` is a different form and is still allowed when the property can be removed.

questions.prompt: A static initialization block runs while the class is being evaluated.

query.title: Static blocks run during class evaluation
query.explanation: A static block runs as part of evaluating the class declaration, in source order with the other static elements. `n` is `1` as soon as the class statement finishes, before any instance is constructed. It does not wait for `new Box()`.

questions.prompt: Default parameter expressions run at call time, not at function-definition time.

query.title: Default expressions run when the function is called
query.explanation: A default expression is evaluated when the call needs it, so `f()` reads the current value of `n` and returns `2`. It is not frozen at the value `n` had when `f` was defined. Each call evaluates the expression again if that argument is missing.

questions.prompt: A destructured parameter can have a default.

query.title: Destructured parameters can default
query.explanation: A parameter pattern can include defaults: `{ a = 1 }` defaults the property, and `= {}` defaults the whole parameter. `f()` therefore returns `1`. Destructured parameters are not limited to required objects with no defaults.

questions.prompt: Object-destructuring rest collects the remaining enumerable own string-keyed properties.

query.title: Object rest keeps enumerable own string keys
query.syntax:
const { a, ...rest } = { a: 1, b: 2, [s]: 3 };
rest; // { b: 2 }
query.explanation: The rest object receives the enumerable own properties whose keys are strings and that were not already pulled out by name. `b` is included, while the symbol key is not, and non-enumerable properties are not either. Rest does not copy the whole property table.

questions.prompt: A microtask queued from inside a microtask runs before any pending timer.

query.title: Nested microtasks drain before the next timer
query.syntax:
queueMicrotask(() => queueMicrotask(inner));
// inner runs before setTimeout
query.explanation: The microtask checkpoint keeps draining the microtask queue until it is empty, including microtasks queued by microtasks. A timer that was already scheduled still waits until that drain finishes. The nested microtask does not get postponed behind the pending macrotask.

questions.prompt: Promise.resolve().then callbacks run before the next setTimeout even if the timeout was queued first.
questions.code:
setTimeout(() => {}, 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => {});

query.title: A then callback jumps ahead of an already queued timer
query.explanation: Queueing a timer first only puts a macrotask on the task queue. A promise reaction queued afterward is still a microtask, and microtasks run before the next macrotask. The earlier `setTimeout` call does not give the timer priority over `.then`.

questions.prompt: Code in an async function before the first await shares the synchronous call stack with the caller.

query.title: Code before the first await runs on the caller stack
query.explanation: Until the first `await`, an async function runs synchronously as part of the call that invoked it, so the caller is still on the stack. Side effects in that prefix happen before the caller continues. The prefix is not deferred onto a microtask; only the continuation after `await` is.
